definition: Fulling, also called milling, finishes woven or knitted wool cloth with moisture, warmth, soap or alkali and mechanical action so it shrinks, thickens and partly felts into a denser fabric.
explanation: Loom-state woolen cloth is open and loose. In fulling it is wetted with a soap or alkaline liquor, sometimes an acid one, and repeatedly compressed, beaten or tumbled. Wool fibers migrate and entangle, drawing the yarns together; the cloth shrinks in length and width, the weave is partly hidden under a felted surface, and the fabric gains mass per area, warmth, wind resistance and resistance to fraying. The operator controls the degree of shrinkage through time, temperature, pH and mechanical intensity, and the cloth is then washed and often raised and cropped.
example: A mill fulls two cloths woven from similar woolen yarns. One is milled lightly so its weave stays visible and crisp. The other is milled heavily until the weave nearly disappears under a dense, felted face suited to an overcoat, as in a melton. Both came off the loom as loose cloth; fulling set their final character.
caution: Fulling is controlled felting of an already constructed fabric, whereas felting from loose fiber makes a textile with no yarns at all. The same shrinkage mechanism is what ruins wool sweaters in a hot machine wash, so fulled cloth can still shrink further if mistreated. Fulling also differs from scouring, which removes grease from raw fiber, although historic fulling cleaned cloth as well.
deeper: Fulling depends on the directional friction that drives felting: the overlapping cuticle scales of wool make a fiber slide more easily in one direction than the other, so repeated compression and release ratchets fibers along and entangles them. Moisture, warmth and soap or alkali swell and lubricate the fibers and speed the process, and some mills mill under acid conditions instead. Modern rotary milling machines drive the cloth in rope form between rollers into a compression chamber, and tumbling machines are also used. Shrink-resist treatments that degrade or mask the scales, as used for machine-washable wool, strongly reduce the response to milling, so superwash wool cannot be fulled in the usual way.
origins: Fulling is ancient. Roman fullers cleaned and finished cloth in workshops using stale urine and absorbent clays, and the clay called fuller's earth takes its name from this use in drawing grease out of wool cloth. In medieval Europe, water-powered fulling mills drove heavy wooden hammers, mechanizing the trade, while in the Scottish Highlands and Islands cloth was fulled by hand in waulking, accompanied by work songs. The English surnames Fuller, Tucker and Walker preserve regional names for the craft.

definition: Gabardine is a firm, warp-faced steep twill cloth, long used for suits, trousers, uniforms and rainwear, and made in wool, cotton or blends.
explanation: In a classic gabardine, warp yarns dominate the face and the twill wale runs at a steep angle, often around 45 to 63 degrees depending on thread counts. The structure packs tightly, so the cloth sheds light rain better than an open plain weave and holds a crease for trousers and jackets. Wool gabardine is a staple of tailored suiting and trench-coat shells; cotton gabardine appears in chinos and workwear. The name identifies a construction family, not a sheep breed or a micron grade, and finishing (piece-dye, stretch, water-repellent coatings) further changes how the cloth behaves.
example: Look at the face of wool suit trousers labeled gabardine: fine diagonal wales climb steeply, the face looks smoother and more warp-rich than the back, and the cloth feels compact between the fingers. Compare that with a softer 2/2 wool twill jacket cloth, where the diagonal is shallower and both systems show more equally. The steep, warp-faced geometry is what mill language is naming, before fiber content or Super numbers enter the conversation.
caution: Gabardine describes weave and face character, not waterproofing, stretch or fiber quality. A cotton gabardine chino and a Super 120s wool gabardine trouser share a structural idea but not performance. Coatings and membranes, not the twill alone, create truly waterproof rainwear. Do not treat gabardine as a synonym for every twill, and do not read the word as proof of virgin wool or a particular origin.
deeper: Steep warp-faced twills such as 2/1 or 3/1 raise warp cover on the face, increasing abrasion resistance along the wearing surface while leaving the back weft-richer. High thread density and fine yarns sharpen the wale and produce the hard, dry hand associated with classic suiting gabardine. Thomas Burberry's late-nineteenth-century gabardine raincoats popularized a tightly woven, yarn-dyed or piece-finished cloth for weatherwear, and the construction later migrated widely into men's trousers and uniforms. Modern stretch gabardines insert elastane in warp or weft, which changes recovery and pressing behavior even when the visual twill remains. Weave notation and measured cover factor still explain more than the marketing noun alone.
origins: The English word gabardine has older garment associations, but as a cloth name it became prominent with tightly woven twill rainwear and suiting in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, including Burberry's weatherproof gabardine. Tailors and mills then used the term for steep warp-faced wool twills in town suits and trousers, separate from softer unfinished tweeds. Cotton gabardine followed into workwear and casual trousers. Today the word travels internationally as a construction label on wool and cotton goods alike, while trademarked rainwear systems remain distinct commercial stories.
